newsitem.title: UK: UK bosses, unions in talks about new union rights.
newsitem.headline: UK bosses, unions in talks about new union rights.

text.p: Talks are underway between British business leaders and trades unions to discuss a proposed law which would require companies to recognise a union if a majority of the workforce wishes to belong, a spokeswoman close to the talks said on Wednesday.
The informal meetings are between the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) and the Trades Union Congress (TUC), the main body for British unions, she said.
The government is reported to be seeking the approval of both these influential bodies for its planned law change, which it expects to draw up by the end of 1997.

"(Union recognition) is the main topic of discussion. It is not something that the CBI has wanted and it has argued quite strongly against changes to industrial legislation earlier this year when there was another government," a CBI spokeswoman told Reuters.
Business argues that formalising a union's role in negotiations will disrupt the existing communication and consultative links between management and workers.
Statutory union recognition would mean companies would be legally bound to bargain with unions on pay conditions, holidays and training. The law does not require them to do so at present.

A TUC spokeswoman confirmed the two sides had held a couple of meetings so far and another was planned, during which a range of issues including the legal right to have a union negotiate on workers' behalf would be discussed.
"They were fairly informal talks and there was no definite outcome or deadline being aimed at," she said.
Business leaders say they are resigned to key employment market changes taking place after the election on May 1 of a new Labour government.
The government is already pushing ahead with plans to set a national minimum wage and with signing up to the European Social Chapter, a framework for laws governing working practices.
"Being realistic, under Labour, these planned changes are likely to happen so it's best to get involved at an early stage," the CBI spokeswoman said.
Recognition is one of the Labour government's main pledges to the unions, which were shackled by a raft of anti-union laws passed under Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government in the 1980s.

However the proposed legislation was not included in the government's legislative timetable for this year. Some union leaders fear the Labour Party is determined to stay distanced from the unions, its traditional paymasters.
The TUC sees union recognition as one of the main planks of its drive to raise its political profile and improve workers' rights.
"One of the key elements of the government's programme for tackling job insecurity must be effective rights to be represented by a trade union," TUC general secretary John Monks said recently.
